title: Healing, Feasting, and Questions of Authority
overview: Jesus heals and forgives a paralyzed man, eats with outsiders, and answers religious teachers who question his authority over forgiveness, fasting and the Sabbath, the weekly day of rest.

parts.label: Friends dig through a roof (vv. 1-5)
parts.note: Houses in the area often had flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, so the four friends could break an opening and lower the man on his mat. Jesus responds to the faith of the whole group, and his first words to the man are not about his body but about his sins being forgiven.

parts.label: Who can forgive sins? (vv. 6-12)
parts.note: The teachers are right that in their scriptures only God forgives sins, so a man claiming to do it sounds like an insult to God. Jesus heals the man as visible proof of the unseen forgiveness, calling himself the Son of Man, a title that likely echoes a figure given authority by God in Daniel 7; Christians read this as Jesus claiming a role that belongs to God.

parts.label: Dinner with tax collectors (vv. 13-17)
parts.note: Tax collectors gathered tolls for the ruling powers and were widely seen as dishonest collaborators, and "sinners" meant people known for not keeping religious law. Eating together signaled acceptance, and Jesus explains it with a doctor's logic: he came for the people who know they need help.

parts.label: Why no fasting? (vv. 18-22)
parts.note: Fasting was a sign of mourning or longing, so Jesus says it makes no sense at a wedding while the groom is present, though one day he will be taken away; Christians read that as a hint of his death. The patch and wineskin images suggest that what he brings will not fit neatly inside old patterns, though how far that reaches is a matter of interpretation.

parts.label: Picking grain on the Sabbath (vv. 23-26)
parts.note: The law let anyone entering a neighbor's field pick grain by hand (Deuteronomy 23:25), but doing it on the Sabbath could count as harvesting, a kind of work forbidden that day. Jesus points to David eating the sacred bread kept for priests (1 Samuel 21), where the priest is actually named as Abiathar's father, Ahimelech, a difference scholars explain in various ways.

parts.label: The Sabbath made for people (vv. 27-28)
parts.note: Jesus says the day of rest was given as a gift for human good, not as a burden people exist to serve. He then claims, as the Son of Man, authority over the Sabbath itself.

disagreement: Christians differ on what Jesus being Lord of the Sabbath means today, some holding that a weekly day of rest is still binding and others that this teaching shows Sabbath rules are no longer required.
think: When have you seen rules or traditions truly help people, and when have you seen them get in the way of someone who needed help?
